extracted.intended_audience: Canadian patent applicants, patent agents, and patent examiners
extracted.subtask_description: Guidance and examination standards for drafting and examining patent claims and determining statutory subject-matter under the Canadian Patent Act and Patent Rules. Covers claim form, support, scope, dependent claims, special claim types, and excluded subject-matter.

rubrics_metrics.name: Negative expressions in claims
rubrics_metrics.description: Claims containing negative expressions such as 'not being...', 'not having...', 'not requiring...' may be objectionable under subsection 27(4) of the Patent Act because claims should generally set forth what the invention is or does, and not what it is not or does not do, unless there is no positive way to describe it.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Avoid negative claim language unless no positive way exists. Dependent claims that effectively cancel or negate features of a preceding claim and thereby make the dependent claim broader than the preceding claim are objectionable under subsection 63(4) of the Patent Rules.

rubrics_metrics.name: Completeness of claims (sufficiency/operability)
rubrics_metrics.description: To define the invention distinctly and in explicit terms, sufficient elements must be recited for operability; the inventive features must appear in each claim.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: In compositions, a claim must define a minimum of two ingredients, at least broadly. Claims failing to recite sufficient elements are indefinite and contrary to subsection 27(4) of the Patent Act.

rubrics_metrics.name: Support by the description
rubrics_metrics.description: A claim must be fully supported by the description as required by section 60 of the Patent Rules; all characteristics of the embodiment set forth in the claim must be fully set forth in the description.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Terms used in claims and description must be used in the same sense; claims are objected to for lack of support if claim terms are not used in the description and cannot be clearly inferred. Originally filed claims are part of the specification and matter in originally filed claims not in the description may be added to the description (subject to divisional application limits).

rubrics_metrics.name: Claims referring to description or drawings
rubrics_metrics.description: It is generally not acceptable for a claim to contain reference to the description or drawings (subsection 62(1) of the Patent Rules), unless the claim itself is complete and can be read and understood without the reference.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Claims must not rely on references such as 'as described in the description' or 'as illustrated in Figure 3' for technical features except where absolutely necessary. Exceptions and permitted references are detailed below (reference numerals, charts/tables/graphs, complex tests, sequence listings/biological deposits).

rubrics_metrics.name: Reference numerals in claims
rubrics_metrics.description: Reference numerals used in the drawings are permissible in a claim provided they are between parentheses (subsection 62(2) of the Patent Rules) and the claim is otherwise explicit and complete.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: If a claim is not complete without referring to parts identified by numerals, it must be objected to as contravening subsection 27(4) of the Patent Act.

rubrics_metrics.name: Reference to charts, tables and graphs
rubrics_metrics.description: Reference to charts, tables or graphs in claims may be permitted where the invention is very complex and it is practically impossible or extremely cumbersome to define relationships precisely without such references.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: If a chart/table is brief and concise (about 5-10 lines), the applicant may be required to enter it into the claims (subsection 62(1)). Use references to large/complex tabulations only where reproduction in the claim would be impractical.

rubrics_metrics.name: Reference to unconventional disclosed tests
rubrics_metrics.description: If an unconventional test can be accurately defined in a few lines it must be included in the claim; if the test is complex and lengthy (e.g. requires more than one page), the applicant may refer to the test as defined in the description.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Short definable tests belong in the claim; lengthy complex tests may be referenced to avoid unwieldy claims.

rubrics_metrics.name: Reference to sequence listings and biological deposits
rubrics_metrics.description: Reference may be made within a claim to sequence listing identifier numbers and biological deposit catalogue numbers (subsections 62(3) and (4) of the Patent Rules).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Follow detailed procedures specified for biotechnology (see chapter 23).

rubrics_metrics.name: Scope of claim relative to description
rubrics_metrics.description: A claim may be as narrow as the applicant wishes within the scope of the invention disclosed, but must not be broader than the invention as described or supported by the description.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Claims should be given the meaning and scope normally used in the relevant art unless the description explicitly gives a special meaning. Claims covering subject-matter outside the scope of the described invention should be objected to for failing to satisfy section 60 of the Patent Rules.

rubrics_metrics.name: Ranges within broader described ranges
rubrics_metrics.description: No objection is made to claims directed to narrower ranges that fall within a broader range described in the description even if the narrow range is not specifically shown in the description.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: If the broad claim is anticipated by prior art, the narrower claim will also fall unless restricting to the narrower range produces a new and unobvious result or effect.

rubrics_metrics.name: Dependent claim formal requirements
rubrics_metrics.description: Section 63 permits claims to refer to one or more other claims to define an invention more narrowly by adding further characteristics; a dependent claim must state the additional features claimed and must only refer to preceding claims by number.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Claims referring to other claims to avoid repetition must not become ambiguous or contravene subsection 27(4). A claim referring to more than one claim must refer to those claims in the alternative only (subsection 63(3)); common phrasing: '…according to any one of claims…'. Examiner should object where there is uncertainty which part of a preceding claim is referred to or where cross-category referencing creates ambiguity.

rubrics_metrics.name: Multiple-claim references and alternatives
rubrics_metrics.description: A claim that refers to more than one claim must do so in the alternative (e.g., 'according to any one of claims 1 to 5').
rubrics_metrics.guidance: References like 'according to any of the above claims' (without numeric alternative) are not acceptable. Examples in the manual illustrate acceptable and unacceptable forms (see claim 7 and claim 11 examples).

rubrics_metrics.name: Page numbering of claims
rubrics_metrics.description: Pages of the claims must be numbered consecutively and run continuously from the last page of the description so that the pages of the specification as a whole are numbered consecutively (subsection 50(1) of the Patent Rules).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Transitional provisions apply for certain filing dates (see section 193 for category 3 applications).

rubrics_metrics.name: Definition and patentability of combinations
rubrics_metrics.description: A combination is a union of elements or process steps cooperating to produce a unitary and practical result that is not the sum of the known characteristics of the elements or steps. A patentable combination is where elements cooperate in an unexpected manner or in a known way to give an unobvious result or effect.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Subcombinations (parts of a combination) may be claimed. Claims to combinations are allowable if they meet Patent Act and Rules requirements.

rubrics_metrics.name: Exhaustive combinations (scope limits)
rubrics_metrics.description: Claims must not exceed the scope of the invention by going further than the protection to which the inventor is entitled; generally, inventor entitled to claim the invention and its immediate and cooperating environment.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Claims to larger environments or downstream combinations are objectionable unless the overall combination produces new and unexpected results amounting to further invention (which may require restriction under section 36).

rubrics_metrics.name: Product claims: acceptable definitions
rubrics_metrics.description: A product may be defined by structure, by the process by which it is made (product-by-process), or by physical or chemical properties; mixtures of these forms are possible.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: The most explicit and definite product claims define the product by structure; where structure is known, it should be given in the claim (subsection 27(4) requirement to distinguish new product).

rubrics_metrics.name: Product-by-process claims
rubrics_metrics.description: A product-by-process claim defines the product wholly or partly in terms of the process used to produce it; process limitations may be included within the product claim or the product claim may be dependent on a process claim.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Use of past participle adjectives (welded, molded, coated) does not convert a product claim into product-by-process. Product-by-process claims must define the product explicitly and distinguish it from known products; they must be directed to the final product of the process claim upon which they depend. Known products cannot be claimed merely by dependency on a new process.

rubrics_metrics.name: Means claims (functional claiming)
rubrics_metrics.description: A 'means' claim defines part of an invention as a means or mechanism for performing an act rather than reciting the element performing the action.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Claims composed of more than one statement of old means can be allowable if there is invention in the new combination. A single statement of means is objectionable as indefinite (subsection 27(4)). A claim is also objected to if it contains a broad means statement at the point of invention that embraces all possible means (merely restates the problem). Examiner should indicate in detail why a means claim is indefinite. Examples illustrate unacceptable 'means for...' and acceptable claims reciting structure.

rubrics_metrics.name: Process and method claim distinction
rubrics_metrics.description: A method is the series of steps to be followed to achieve a desired result; a process includes the method and the substances to which it is applied. The overall process can be new even if the method is old.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: A claim to a process applying a known method to known substances can be patentable if the method has never been applied to those substances and results in new, useful, and unobvious products.

rubrics_metrics.name: Method-of-use and use claims (including medicinal use limits)
rubrics_metrics.description: Claims to a method of use or a use of a compound may be allowable when a compound claim is allowable; however method-of-medical-treatment claims are rejected under case law (e.g., Tennessee Eastman) and Section 2 considerations.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Claims to obvious uses of known compounds should be objected to for lacking patentable subject-matter; claims to new and unobvious uses are allowable. Method-of-use claims directed to industrial uses are allowable but must include manipulative steps to distinguish from mere use claims. Method claims for medical treatment are not accepted; product claims containing a medical treatment step are not accepted (example contrasts accepted 'use as herbicide' with not accepted 'use for treatment of patients intravenously').

rubrics_metrics.name: Guidelines for use claims incorporating steps
rubrics_metrics.description: Use claims are permitted and use claims incorporating method steps are acceptable provided the use is clearly identified and not a method of medical treatment.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: If the claim is complete and understandable without method steps, the claim as a whole is acceptable; method steps serve only to restrict a previously recited use.

rubrics_metrics.name: Markush claims (genus claims)
rubrics_metrics.description: A Markush claim (a genus expressed as 'selected from the group consisting of...') is allowable in chemical cases provided it is clear that the alternatives possess at least one property in common mainly responsible for their function in the claimed relationship.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Markush format may occasionally be used in mechanical/electrical fields. A Markush should generally cover a group of two or more different materials/elements/compounds with a common functional property; examples given (solvent selected from alcohol, ether, acetone).

rubrics_metrics.name: Statutory subject-matter categories (section 2)
rubrics_metrics.description: To be statutory, subject-matter must fall within one of the categories in section 2 of the Patent Act: art, process, machine, manufacture or composition of matter, or a new and useful improvement in any of these categories.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Determine whether the subject-matter is proper 'subject-matter' for a patent by asking whether it falls within these statutory categories.

rubrics_metrics.name: Definition of 'art' (useful/practical art)
rubrics_metrics.description: An 'art' pertains to the application of knowledge to effect a desired result; to be statutory, an 'art' must be a 'useful art' and a 'manual or productive art'.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: An art must be the practical application of knowledge and is typically claimed as either a use or a method. Use claims set out a manner of employing something to accomplish a result; method claims include particular steps required to achieve the result.

rubrics_metrics.name: Definition of 'process'
rubrics_metrics.description: A 'process' implies the application of a method to a material or materials; it is a mode or method of operation producing a result by physical or chemical action or by application of one substance to another.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Whether a process is statutory is not determined by whether it produces a statutory product.

rubrics_metrics.name: Definition of 'machine', 'manufacture', and 'composition of matter'
rubrics_metrics.description: Machine: mechanical/physical embodiment of functions where parts cooperate to accomplish an effect; Manufacture: broadly a non-living mechanistic product or process of making technical articles; Composition of matter: physical/chemical substances, compounds and compositions including combinations of ingredients.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Machines may be claimed as device/apparatus/system. Manufactures are articles made by physical labour or mechanical power (often modern industrial production). 'Composition' implies ingredients perceptible in space and mass; scope limited to avoid redundancy with 'machine' and 'manufacture'.

rubrics_metrics.name: Inventions must not be disembodied (practical form requirement)
rubrics_metrics.description: An invention is a solution to a practical problem and must have physical existence or manifest a discernible effect or change — a 'practical' or 'practicable' form — to be patentable.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: A disembodied idea, concept or discovery is not patentable unless incorporated in a practical form (e.g., has a method of practical application). Case law illustrates that the idea that leads to an invention is not the invention; invention involves the something further that produces a new product, process, result or combination.

rubrics_metrics.name: Excluded subject-matter: scientific principles and abstract theorems
rubrics_metrics.description: No patent shall be granted for any mere scientific principle or abstract theorem (subsection 27(8) of the Patent Act). Courts interpret this to exclude mathematical formulae, natural phenomena and laws of nature when claimed in a general sense.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Exclusion applies when attempting to claim the abstract principle itself, but not when a scientific principle, law of nature or mathematical formula is relied upon in operating a practical form of an invention.
